# Writing a VU1 program

The PlayStation 2 draws through **VU1**, a vector unit running a microprogram
over every vertex. A TyraX project can replace the engine's microprogram with
its own, and it is written in **ordinary C++** — no assembly.

Put a `.cpp` under `src/vu/`. That is the whole setup: the editor notices it and
copies the framework in next to it (`vugen/`), and the build compiles and runs
it.

```cpp
#include "vushader.hpp"

namespace {
struct Posterize : vu::Program {
  const char* name() const override { return "Posterize"; }
  unsigned classes() const override { return vu::kAll; }
  vu::Slot slot() const override { return vu::Slot::Color; }

  void vertex(vu::Ctx& c) override {
    c.color.rgb() = vu::quantize(c, c.color, 5.0F);
  }
};
}  // namespace
VU_PROGRAM(Posterize);
```

## The one thing to understand first

**Your C++ does not run on the PS2. It runs on the build machine, once, and
what it leaves behind is a microprogram.**

`vertex()` is not called per vertex at run time — it is called while the program
is being *built*, and every operation you write (`c.color * k`, `b.mulInto(...)`)
**appends an instruction**. The C++ is a description. That is why a mistake is an
ordinary compiler error with your own file and line number, and why a loop in
`vertex()` is unrolled rather than executed.

## Slots — where in the pipeline the body runs

`slot()` is the whole of what you have to know about the pipeline.

| Slot | The position is | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `ObjectSpace` | the mesh's own units, before the transform | displacement (waves, inflation) |
| `ClipSpace` | after the MVP; **w is the view distance** | depth-driven effects |
| `Ndc` | after the perspective divide, before the screen conversion | screen-space effects (snapping) |
| `Color` | the vertex colour, before it is clamped | **the default**, and where most effects belong |
| `Texture` | the ST, before perspective correction | UV scrolling |

Do not guess a slot's range — copy the numbers from a stage in the catalogue
that already works in it. `Slot::Ndc` in particular is *not* a −1..1 cube here.

## Material classes — a program replaces a CLASS, not an object

VU1 micro memory has no room for a program per object, so a program is installed
over a **material class** and draws every mesh of it:

| `vu::` constant | Meshes |
|---|---|
| `kColour` | vertex colour only — the fallback for everything |
| `kLit` | shaded on VU1 from the scene's lights |
| `kLitTextured` | the same, with a texture |
| `kTextured` | vertex colour + a texture |
| `kMatcap` | a `refl` material; the ST slot carries a normal |
| `kAll` | all five |

**A program that MOVES geometry must claim `kAll`.** One object often draws
several passes over the same vertices in different classes — a reflective ball
has a base pass and a matcap pass, and a baked lightmap is a *textured* bag even
on an untextured mesh. Displace one and not the other and the copies separate,
each showing through the other.

## Per-mesh parameters

Four floats per object (`c.params.x()` … `.w()`), set in the editor's Properties
panel or from a script (`obj.data.vuParams[i]`) with no rebuild. The kind of
effect is per class; its **strength** is per mesh. `c.time` is a clock
`(seconds, sin, cos, 1.0)`, already range-reduced.

One restriction: those four numbers live where a lit program keeps its light
colours, so a program that **binds a parameter** cannot claim `kLit` or
`kLitTextured`. A program using plain values may claim anything.

## The rules that cost a console build to learn

The VS Code extension reports the first four in the Problems panel as you type —
if you see one of these underlined, it is not a false positive.

- **Never divide.** `divQ`, `rsqrtQ` and anything else writing Q. Q carries the
  perspective divide and the assembler schedules around its latency, so a divide
  from your body gets moved into that window and vertices land in the wrong
  place. On the console: grey stippled patches. On the host: nothing wrong at
  all. Compute it another way.
- **There are four scratch registers** (`c.scratch(0..3)`). Asking for a fifth
  silently aliases the fourth.
- **A geometry slot needs `movesGeometry()`** returning true. Without it the
  clipper cuts the mesh before your program runs and props tear at the edge of
  the screen.
- **Do not write the position at `Slot::Color` or `Texture`** — by then it is a
  screen-space integer, not a position.
- **The register ceiling is real and it is not micro memory.** A lit program
  already keeps ~30 of the 31 float registers live, so a third heavy stage on
  one program tends to fail inside the assembler with `no opt table` and no line
  number. Split the effect across two material classes, or write it more
  cheaply.
- **A wavelength shorter than a mesh tears that mesh open.** Displacement moves
  a mesh's own vertices by different amounts; long waves lift whole objects,
  which is what water looks like.

## Turning one on, and the budget

By default a program installs at boot. The **checkbox** in *Tools > VU Programs*
sets that per script, or the script decides for itself:

```cpp
bool activeAtBoot() const override { return false; }
```

A script that overrides the method wins and the panel greys its checkbox — that
is C++ doing what C++ does with a virtual, not a rule the framework invented.

At run time the game switches programs with
`vuscript::activate(vuscript::kMyProgram)` / `deactivate` / `deactivateAll`. The
index constants come from `name()`. **Only what is ACTIVE occupies micro
memory**, which is what lets a game carry more programs than fit at once — the
cost of a switch is one pipeline drain and one upload, so it belongs on an event
and never in a per-frame update.

*Tools > VU Programs > Micro memory* is the budget: 2042 usable instruction
slots for the whole resident set. Overrunning it in a release build overwrites a
helper the post-effect chain needs and hangs the frame, so check the bar before
shipping. A script's numbers there come from the last **build** — the editor has
no compiler to run your C++ with, and the panel says so.

## Where to look

- `src/vu/*.cpp` in this project — the working examples, and the fastest way in.
- `vugen/vushader.hpp` — the authoring surface: `vu::Ctx`, `vu::Vec`, the free
  functions (`splat`, `constant`, `saturate`, `quantize`, `lerp`, `dot3`), and
  `c.raw()` for the whole builder underneath. Every member is documented there;
  it is the reference, not this file.
- The generated microprogram lands in `src/gen/vu_script*.vclpp` after a build —
  readable, and the VS Code extension gives every instruction a hover.
